title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: If we assume, as historians do, that great men lead humanity toward the attainment of certain goals—the greatness of Russia or of France, the balance of power in Europe, the spread of revolutionary ideas, general progress, or anything else—then it is impossible to explain the facts of history without resorting to the concepts of "chance" and "genius."

If the goal of the European wars at the start of the nineteenth century had been the expansion of Russia, that goal could have been achieved without all the preceding wars and without the invasion. If the goal had been the expansion of France, that goal could have been reached without the Revolution and without the Empire. If the goal had been the spread of ideas, the printing press would have accomplished that far better than soldiers. If the goal had been the progress of civilization, one can easily imagine that there were other paths to spreading civilization besides the destruction of people and their wealth.
Why did it happen this way and not some other?
Because it just happened that way! "Chance created the situation; genius made use of it," says history.
But what is chance? What is genius?

The words "chance" and "genius" do not refer to anything that actually exists, and therefore cannot be defined. They only indicate a certain stage in our understanding of events. I don't know why a certain event occurs; I think I cannot know; so I don't try to know, and I say: "chance." I see a force producing effects beyond the scope of ordinary human powers; I don't understand why this happens, and I say: "genius."

To a flock of sheep, the ram that the shepherd drives each evening into a special pen to be fattened—growing twice as fat as the rest—must seem like a genius. And it must appear an astonishing combination of genius with a whole series of extraordinary coincidences that this ram, instead of entering the common pen each evening, ends up in a special one where he gets extra oats, and that this particular ram, swelling with fat, is eventually killed for mutton.

But the sheep only need to stop assuming that everything happening to them is designed for their sheepish purposes; they only need to admit that what happens to them may serve purposes beyond their understanding—and they will immediately see a unity and coherence in what is being done to the fattened ram. Even if they don't know why he's being fattened, at least they'll know that everything that happens to the ram doesn't happen by accident, and they'll have no need for the concepts of "chance" or "genius."

Only by giving up our claim to understand some immediately obvious purpose, and accepting that the ultimate purpose is beyond our grasp, can we see the chain of experiences in the lives of historical figures and perceive the cause of the effect they produce, which is disproportionate to their ordinary human abilities. Only then will we have no need for the words "chance" and "genius."

We need only acknowledge that we do not know the purpose of the European upheavals, and that we only know the facts—that is, the killings, first in France, then in Italy, Africa, Prussia, Austria, Spain, and Russia—and that the movements from west to east and from east to west form the essential substance of those events. Only then will we no longer need to see something exceptional—some stroke of genius—in the characters of Napoleon and Alexander, and will no longer need to attribute the event to some individual's specific quality.

By abandoning any claim to knowledge of the ultimate purpose, we will clearly see that just as it's impossible to imagine a blossom or seed better suited to a plant than the one it actually produces, so too it's impossible to imagine any two people more perfectly adapted, down to the smallest detail, to fulfill the roles that Napoleon and Alexander played.
